dataset.title: 1750 to 2010 Refractory Black Carbon Deposition from a Global Ice-Core Array, Arctic, Antarctic, and alpine regions

abstract.para: Refractory black carbon (rBC) aerosols in air and precipitation result from incomplete combustion. Prior to 18th century industrialization, the primary emission sources were wildfires and agricultural fires. After industrialization, fossil fuel burning has become an important emission source as well. Because these aerosols are import contributors to Earth’s radiative forcing both in the air and when deposited to bright surfaces such as fresh snow, quantifying past rBC emissions is critical to accurate Earth System Modeling. This data set contains 1750 to 2010 annual rBC depositional fluxes measured in a global array of 31, mostly polar ice cores. They were used (Zhang et al., Nature Communications, 2024) to reconstruct atmospheric rBC emissions using the atmospheric chemical transport GEOS-Chem. Details on the rBC measurement methods and chronology development are provided in the associated references for the individual ice core records.

section.title: Ethical Research Practices
section.para: Although permits may have been required to collect the ice cores and interactions with local communities and authorities may have occurred at that time, the measurements reported here were made on archived ice-core samples many years after collection and did not involve fieldwork. Therefore, no permits or institutional review board approvals were required for this research, and there were no interactions with local communities or authorities. In addition, this research did not involve any sensitive materials or data (e.g., archaeological or other historical materials, human or animal remains or subjects) and had no impact on local or nearby communities.

description.para: These measurements were made on samples from 31 recently collected cores from the Arctic and Antarctic, or on samples from archived ice cores obtained from U.S. and international institutions and universities.

The ice cores in this global area were collected from 31 Arctic, Antarctic, and alpine sites. For the 29 ice cores analyzed at the Desert Research Institute, measurements were made on a continuous ice core melter system with an effective depth resolution of 1 to 1.5 centimeter(cm). Ice cores from 2 sites were analyzed at the Paul Scherrer Institut in Switzerland using discrete sampling techniques with ~1.5 cm depth resolution.

samplingDescription.para: For continuous rBC measurements at the Desert Research Institute, longitudinal samples with a cross section of ~0.032 by ~0.032 meter (m) cores were cut from the ice cores at the 29 drill sites and the ends decontaminated by scraping with a precleaned ceramic knife. The samples were analyzed for rBC using the continuous ice-core analytical system at the Desert Research Institute (DRI) using methods described in detail elsewhere (McConnell et al., 2007, Science, doi:10.1126/science.1144856; Bisiaux et al., 2012, Atmos Chem Phys, doi:10.5194/acp-12-4109-2012; McConnell et al., 2021, Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03858-9). In brief, the DRI BC method used here coupled a Cetac U5000AT Ultrasonic Nebulizer (USN) or an APEX-Q (Elemental Scientific) Desolating Nebulizer to a Single Particle Soot Photometer (SP2; Droplet Measurement Technologies, Boulder, CO, USA) for high-time-resolution, continuous determinations of rBC concentration in real time since measurements were made approximately 3 minutes after the ice core was melted. Five BC standards were made from sequential dilutions of Cabojet 200, ranging in concentration from ~0.1 to ~6.0 nanograms per gram (ng g−1). Standards were measured at the beginning and end of each analysis day, with ~1.0 ng g−1 quality control standards analyzed every ~2.5 hours (h) during routine pauses in the continuous ice core analyses for calibration of the analytical system. The rBC measurements were combined to annual averages and fluxes calculated following standard procedures (i.e., each annual average concentration was multiplied by the corresponding annual water-equivalent accumulation). rBC flux uncertainties in the ice core records are estimated to be less than 5%.
For the discrete measurements made at the Paul Scherrer Institute, analytical details are given in Sigl et al., 2018, The Cryosphere, doi:10.5194/tc-12-3311-2018.
